title: EST English — Full Practice Test 2
kicker: American Diploma · EST I · Practice test
summary: A second full, timed EST I English practice test: Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language, 44 questions, 35 minutes) and Literacy Test 2 (Reading, 52 questions, 65 minutes), with an explanation for every answer choice.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice version of the two English parts of EST I: **Literacy Test 1 (Writing and Language)** and **Literacy Test 2 (Reading)**. Every passage and question was written for this site by Mohamed Abdelkriem. The test is modelled on the skills that the EST Literacy tests measure; it is not made of official EST questions, and the real test may present questions in a different way.

rows: Four essays with numbered, underlined parts. Fix grammar and punctuation, and improve transitions, order, wording and relevance.
Five long passages (family fiction, history, science with a table, a pair of opinion texts, humanities). Answer questions about ideas, details, words, structure, evidence and data.

blocks.text: These figures are as published by schools; check the latest official EST candidate guide on est.moe.gov.eg before your test.

items: Sit in a quiet place with no phone, no dictionary and no help, exactly as in the real test.
Do the two sections in one sitting if you can. The timer starts when you begin each section and the section ends when the time is up.
Work through the questions in order. You can mark a question and come back to it while the section is still open, but once a section ends you cannot return to it, just as in the real test.
Answer every question. A blank is always wrong; a careful guess may be right.

Each passage is repeated above each of its questions. In Literacy Test 1, only the part that question asks about is underlined and numbered. In Literacy Test 2, the paragraphs are numbered [1], [2], [3] so that questions can point to them.
At the end you see a practice percentage for each section. It is not an official EST scaled score; use it to measure your progress from one practice test to the next.

questions.p:
**The Bucket and the Beam**
Long before engines and electric pumps, Egyptian farmers faced a stubborn problem. The Nile flowed in its channel, but many fields lay above the level of the __[1] river, the__ crops on those fields needed a steady supply of water, especially in the hot months after the flood had gone down. The answer was the shaduf, a simple lifting machine that have been used along the river for thousands of years.
A shaduf is made of a long wooden pole balanced on an upright frame, much like a see-saw. A bucket hangs from a rope at one end of the pole. At the other end a heavy weight, usually a lump of dried mud or a stone. To use it, the farmer pulls the rope down until the bucket dips into the river. Then he lets go, and the weight swings the full bucket up into the air with very little effort. He turns the pole and empties the water into a channel that carries it to the crops. A skilled worker can repeat this movement hundreds of times in a day.
The shaduf is clever because it does most of the grunt work for the farmer. Lifting a full bucket straight up from the river would quickly tire anyone, but on a shaduf the counterweight, which balances the weight of the full bucket does most of the pulling. The device also has clear limits. It can raise water only a short distance, perhaps two or three metres, and it cannot move large amounts quickly. Similarly, farmers who needed more water turned to the sakia, a large wheel turned by an ox or a buffalo.
Today, diesel and electric pumps have replaced most of these old devices. Yet the shaduf has not completely disappeared. In a few villages, and in paintings on the walls of ancient tombs, it's familiar shape can still be seen: a long arm rising upward and lifting up into the air above the green fields. Many tourists visit Egypt every year to see its temples and tombs.
questions.q: [1] Choose the best version of the underlined part.
c: NO CHANGE

questions.e: "Many fields lay above the level of the river" and "the crops on those fields needed a steady supply" are both complete sentences, so they must be separated, here by a full stop. The comma alone (NO CHANGE) creates a comma splice, and the comma after "and" is not allowed.
ce: Two complete sentences joined by a comma alone make a comma splice.
The comma after "and" is wrong and breaks the link between the two clauses.
With no punctuation, the two sentences run together (a run-on).
Correct: a full stop separates the two complete sentences.

questions.p:
**Watching Atoms Move**
Most chemical reactions happen far too quickly for the human eye to follow. When two molecules meet, __[12] they're__ bonds can break and new ones can form in a tiny fraction of a second. For most of the twentieth century, chemists could study what went into a reaction and what came out of it, but the moment of change itself remained hidden. The Egyptian scientist Ahmed Zewail who helped to bring that hidden moment into view.
Zewail was born in 1946 in Damanhur, a city in the Nile Delta. He studied chemistry at Alexandria University and then travelled to the United States, where he earned his doctorate at the University of Pennsylvania. He later joined the California Institute of Technology, where he built the laboratory that would make him famous.
The problem Zewail set out to solve was one of speed. The key steps of a reaction are measured in femtoseconds, and a femtosecond is one millionth of one billionth of a second. No ordinary camera has ever came close to that. Zewail's team used a different tool: extremely short flashes of laser light. The first flash started the reaction, and a second flash, arriving a few femtoseconds later, recorded the position of the atoms at that instant. By repeating the experiment with slightly different delays, the team could put together a series of snapshots, it showed the reaction step by step, much like the frames of a film.
This method, now called femtochemistry, changed the way scientists study reactions. questions.p:
**Rest Is Part of the Training**
Many young athletes believe that the harder they train, the faster they will improve. They run extra laps after practice, skip rest days and feel guilty whenever they take a break. This attitude is understandable, but it rests on a misunderstanding. Training does not make the body stronger by __[23] itself; it__ creates the conditions for the body to grow stronger during rest.
During hard exercise, muscles are put under strain, and tiny areas of damage appear in their fibres. In the hours and days that follow, the body repairs this damage and builds the muscle back slightly stronger than before. Energy stores in the muscles is also refilled, and the nervous system recovers from the effort of the session. When an athlete trains hard day after day without enough rest. The result is not greater strength but growing tiredness.
Coaches call this condition overtraining. An overtrained athlete may feel tired even after a full night's sleep, losing interest in practice and find that performances get worse instead of better. Injuries also become more common, because tired muscles and joints are less able to absorb the shock of running and jumping. In contrast, the athlete who never rests may end up resting the longest, while waiting for an injury to heal.
Rest does not have to mean lying on the sofa all day. Many coaches recommend active recovery; gentle swimming, walking or stretching that keeps the body moving without adding new strain. Sleep matters most of all, above all other things. Much of the body's repair work takes place during deep sleep, so a teenager who stays up late before a match is messing up the very process that training depends on.
None of this means that hard training is bad. Effort, is still the engine of improvement. But an engine that never stops eventually breaks down. Some sports, such as swimming, use different muscles from running.

questions.p:
**The Night Before Eid**
Every year, on the last nights of Ramadan, my __[34] grandmothers'__ small kitchen in Shubra became the busiest room in Cairo. My aunts, my mother and all six of my cousins crowded around the table, and the air smelled of warm butter and sugar. We were there to make kahk, the round Eid biscuits that my grandmother has baked since she was a girl.
My job, as the youngest, was to press patterns into the tops of the biscuits with a small metal tool called a mangash, it looked like a pair of tweezers with tiny teeth. At first, my patterns were crooked and uneven. Some biscuits had deep scratches across their tops; others had none at all. My grandmother never corrected me in front of the others. Instead, she would take my hand in hers and guide it slowly around the edge of the dough, so that the tool left a ring of tiny, even marks.
Around midnight, the trays went into the oven, and the kitchen grew so hot that we opened every window. While we waited, my grandmother told stories about Eids from her childhood, such as: the year the electricity failed and the biscuits were baked in a neighbour's oven, and the year her brother ate a whole tray before dawn. My cousins had heard these stories so many times that they had heard them again and again, but nobody ever interrupted her.
Kahk can be stored for several weeks in a metal tin. My grandmother lifted one biscuit and checked out the pattern on top. It was one of mine. The ring of marks around its edge—every tooth of the mangash pressed to the same depth, was perfectly even. She said nothing; she only smiled and handed it to me, still warm, to dust with sugar.
Now, many years later, my grandmother's hands are too stiff to hold the mangash, so I press the patterns while she watches from her chair. Sometimes, when one of my cousins' children makes a crooked ring, I take the small hand in mine and guide it slowly around the edge of the dough.

**Passage 1 (Literary fiction).** This passage is adapted from an original short story. Hana's older brother, Karim, is about to leave the family's flat in Cairo to begin university in Alexandria.
**The Suitcase in the Hall**
[1] For three days the suitcase had stood in the hall, and for three days everyone in the flat had walked around it as though it were a piece of furniture that had always been there. Nobody mentioned it. Hana's mother stepped over its handle on her way to the kitchen; her father moved it a few centimetres to the left each morning so that he could open the front door, and moved it back again each evening. Only Hana stared at it openly. It was blue, with one wheel that squeaked, and it was the largest thing Karim had ever owned.
[2] On the last evening, her mother cooked as if a wedding were coming. There was molokhia, there was rice with vermicelli, there were stuffed vine leaves that had taken the whole afternoon, and there was a tray of basbousa cooling on the windowsill. "He will not eat like this in Alexandria," her mother said to no one in particular, and filled another container to squeeze into the suitcase. Karim protested that the university had a dining hall, that Alexandria was not a desert, that he would be home in a month. His mother answered each protest by adding another container.
[3] Her father said very little at dinner. He had never been a man for speeches. When Karim had passed his final examinations in the summer, their father had read the results twice, folded the paper carefully, and gone out to buy oranges, which he then handed out to the neighbours without explanation. Hana had been nine when she first understood that her father's feelings came out of him sideways, through his hands rather than his mouth: in a bicycle chain oiled before anyone asked, a broken lamp mended overnight, a school bag that appeared one morning with its torn strap neatly stitched.
[4] After dinner Karim went out to the balcony, and after a moment Hana followed him. The street below was loud with the usual evening noise: a vegetable seller calling out the last of his tomatoes, a boy on a motorbike, two women arguing pleasantly about the price of bread. Karim was leaning on the rail, looking at none of it.
[5] "You can have my room," he said, without turning round.
[6] Hana had wanted his room for as long as she could remember. It had the window that caught the morning sun and the shelf above the bed where he kept his books in careful rows. She had imagined winning it in many ways, most of them dramatic. Now that it was offered, she found that she did not want it at all.
[7] "I'll keep it tidy for you," she said instead, "for when you come back."
[8] Karim laughed, but the laugh came out wrong, and he looked at the street for a while longer before he answered. "Keep it messy," he said. "Otherwise I won't recognise it."
[9] In the morning, the suitcase was gone from the hall before Hana woke. She found it already downstairs beside the taxi, and her father beside it, crouching with a small screwdriver in his hand. The squeaking wheel, she saw, had been taken off and put back on again; when Karim pulled the case towards the car, it rolled across the pavement in perfect silence.
[10] "There," her father said, standing up and brushing the dust from his knees. That was all. But Hana saw Karim look down at the wheel, and then at their father, and she understood that something had been said after all.
[11] When the taxi had turned the corner, the family climbed the stairs without speaking. The hall looked enormous. Hana's mother stood in the kitchen doorway with a container in her hands, the last one, which had not fitted into anything, and for a moment nobody moved. Then her father took it gently from her, opened it, and the three of them stood in the hall eating basbousa with their fingers.
questions.q: Which choice best describes what happens in the passage?
c: A father tries to stop his son from moving to another city for university.
A brother and sister argue over who will have the larger bedroom.
A mother persuades her son to stay at home because she fears he will not eat well.
A family prepares for and reacts to an older son's departure, with each member showing feelings in a different way.
questions.e: The whole story follows how each family member handles Karim's leaving: food, a repaired wheel, a joke about the room. The mother's worry about food is real, but she never tries to keep him at home.
ce: The father helps Karim leave by mending the suitcase.
There is no argument; Karim offers the room and Hana no longer wants it.
She worries about his food, but she never asks him to stay.
Correct: the mother cooks, the father mends, and Hana and Karim speak indirectly about his leaving.

questions.p:
**Passage 3 (Science).** This passage is adapted from an original article about water and exercise in hot weather. The study described is fictional, and its data are for practice only.
**Thirsty Legs**
[1] Football coaches have long told their players to drink plenty of water, but on a hot afternoon many young athletes still arrive at training having drunk little since breakfast. Thirst, it turns out, is a late and unreliable warning. By the time a person feels clearly thirsty, the body may already have lost a noticeable amount of water through sweat, and in hot weather an active teenager can lose more than a litre in an hour of hard exercise.
[2] Why does this matter for performance? Blood is mostly water, and when the body loses fluid, the volume of blood falls. The heart must then beat faster to deliver the same amount of oxygen to working muscles, while also sending blood to the skin to release heat. These two demands compete with each other. As a result, a dehydrated athlete tends to tire sooner, feel hotter and find that tasks requiring both speed and concentration become harder.
[3] To measure how much these effects matter for young players, a team of sports scientists led by Omar Fawzy studied forty members of school football teams, aged fifteen to seventeen, during an unusually hot month. Each player took part in four identical training sessions on separate days. Before each session, the players were weighed; after it, they were weighed again, and the difference, after allowing for anything they had drunk, showed how much water they had lost. The researchers controlled how much water each player drank during the sessions, so that body-water loss ranged from almost nothing to about three percent of body weight. At the end of each session, players ran a set of five sprints and completed a passing test in which they had to hit small targets with the ball.
Table: Average results for the 40 players at four levels of body-water loss
Body-water loss (% of body weight) | Time for five sprints (seconds) | Passes on target (out of 20) | Heart rate at end of session (beats per minute)
Under 0.5 | 28.4 | 16.1 | 168
1 | 28.7 | 15.8 | 172
2 | 29.6 | 14.2 | 179
3 | 30.9 | 12.5 | 186
[4] The results showed a clear pattern. Losing about one percent of body weight made little difference: sprint times and passing accuracy were almost the same as when players were fully hydrated. Beyond that point, however, performance declined steadily. At three percent, the players took 2.5 seconds longer to complete their sprints and hit the target with fewer passes, while their hearts were working noticeably harder.
[5] Fawzy points out that the passing results may matter as much as the sprint times. "Football is a game of decisions," he says. "A player who is a little slower can still be useful. A player who keeps giving the ball away cannot." The fall in passing accuracy suggests that losing water affects not only the legs but also attention and coordination, although the study was not designed to separate these effects.
[6] The team also stresses the limits of its findings. All of the players were healthy boys from three schools in one city, and the sessions took place in hot weather; the results may differ for other groups or in cooler conditions. Drinking far more water than the body needs is not helpful either, and in rare cases it can be dangerous. The researchers' practical advice is simple: players should begin training already well hydrated, drink small amounts regularly during breaks and replace what they have lost after training, without waiting for thirst to tell them when.

questions.p:
**Passage 4 (Paired texts).** Text 1 and Text 2 are original opinion pieces about the place of competitive sport in secondary schools.
**Text 1**
[1] Every secondary school should give each of its students a place on a team. I do not mean a place in a fitness class or a turn on a running machine; I mean a real team that trains together, plays matches against other schools and cares about the result. Exercise can be done alone. The lessons of competitive sport cannot.
[2] On a team, a student learns that his or her effort matters to other people. A defender who stops running lets down ten teammates, not just herself. Young people who learn this early carry it into classrooms and, later, into workplaces, where most success also depends on doing one's part in a group. Competition adds a second lesson: how to lose. A student who has lost a match in front of classmates, shaken hands with the winners and come back to training the next week has practised a kind of resilience that no lecture can teach.
[3] Critics say that competition makes less talented students miserable. Some of it does, when coaches care only about winning and leave the weakest players on the bench. But the solution is better coaching, not less competition. Schools can enter several teams at different levels, so that every student plays regularly against opponents of similar ability. A close match between two modest teams is just as exciting, and just as educational, as a final between champions.
[4] Schools spend a great deal of effort preparing students for examinations that measure what they know. They should spend at least some of it preparing them for the moments when knowledge is not enough: when the score is level, the time is short and the team is relying on them.
**Text 2**
[1] Supporters of compulsory team sport often describe its benefits in glowing terms, and for the students who enjoy it, many of those benefits are real. The trouble is that a school's physical education programme exists for every student, not only for the confident and the naturally athletic.
[2] For a sizeable number of teenagers, a competitive match is not a lesson in resilience but a weekly public embarrassment. They are picked last, shouted at for mistakes and reminded, in front of their classmates, that they are not good at something. Many respond in the most sensible way available to them: they stop taking part as soon as they are allowed to, and some never return to regular exercise at all. A programme that leaves students with a lifelong dislike of physical activity has failed at its most important task.
[3] That task is not to produce winners but to produce adults who move. The habits that keep people healthy in middle age are rarely team sports; they are walking, cycling, swimming, dancing and working out at home or in a gym, activities that can be done alone or with a friend, at any level of skill. Schools should give students a chance to try many of these and to find one they genuinely enjoy.
[4] None of this means that school teams should disappear. Students who love competition should have every opportunity to compete. But competition works best as a choice. Forcing it on everyone risks turning the students who need exercise most into the people who avoid it longest.

**Passage 5 (Humanities).** This passage is adapted from an original essay about the scholar Ibn al-Haytham and the study of light.
**Seeing in the Dark**
[1] Around the year 1000, the most widely accepted ideas about vision would strike a modern reader as strange. Many scholars, following thinkers of ancient Greece, believed that the eye sent out invisible rays that travelled to objects and, in some way, felt them. Others argued that objects sent out tiny copies of themselves, which flew through the air and entered the eye. Both views had distinguished defenders; neither had been tested in any careful way.
[2] Into this debate came Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra, in what is now Iraq, in about 965. He spent much of his working life in Cairo, then the capital of the Fatimid state. According to a story told by later writers, he first came to Egypt with a bold promise: he claimed that the Nile's flood could be controlled by works built in the south. When he travelled up the river and saw the size of the task, the story goes, he realised that the plan was impossible, and to escape the anger of the caliph he pretended to be mad until the ruler's death. Whether every detail of this story is true is uncertain. What is certain is that in Cairo he produced a body of work that would shape the study of light for centuries.
[3] His greatest achievement, the Book of Optics, began by rejecting the idea of rays leaving the eye. Light, he argued, travels from luminous sources such as the sun or a flame, strikes objects, and is reflected from every point on them in straight lines; vision occurs when some of this light enters the eye. He supported his argument not only with reasoning but with observation. Anyone who looks at the sun, he noted, feels pain in the eye, which suggests that something is entering the eye from outside rather than leaving it.
[4] What makes Ibn al-Haytham remarkable is less any single conclusion than the way he reached his conclusions. Again and again, he designed arrangements of equipment to test his claims. He passed light through narrow openings, observed it in darkened rooms and set up tubes and screens to show that light moves in straight lines. In one well-known set of observations, he noted that when light from several lamps passed through a small hole into a dark room, each lamp produced its own separate patch of light on the far wall, and that covering one lamp removed only its patch. The lights, in other words, did not mix in the air. Historians still debate how far Ibn al-Haytham's methods resemble the modern scientific method, and it would be a mistake to treat any single person as its inventor. But it is difficult to read his work without recognising a familiar attitude: the conviction that, when an argument and an experiment disagree, it is the argument that must give way.
questions.q: In paragraph [6], the statement that "it would be a mistake to treat any single person as its inventor" mainly functions to
c: suggest that historians have proved his methods were unscientific.
introduce a different scholar who invented the scientific method.
limit the author's praise by admitting that the scientific method had many contributors.
reject the idea that Ibn al-Haytham's work had any influence in Europe.
questions.e: After praising Ibn al-Haytham, the author adds a fair limit: no one person invented the scientific method. The paragraph still says his book influenced Europe, so the second choice contradicts it.
ce: Historians "still debate" the question; nothing is proved.
No other scholar is named.
Correct: it balances the praise with a fair qualification.
The same paragraph says his book was studied in Europe for centuries.

questions.p:
**Passage 5 (Humanities).** This passage is adapted from an original essay about the scholar Ibn al-Haytham and the study of light.
**Seeing in the Dark**
[1] Around the year 1000, the most widely accepted ideas about vision would strike a modern reader as strange. Many scholars, following thinkers of ancient Greece, believed that the eye sent out invisible rays that travelled to objects and, in some way, felt them. Others argued that objects sent out tiny copies of themselves, which flew through the air and entered the eye. Both views had distinguished defenders; neither had been tested in any careful way.
[2] Into this debate came Abu Ali al-Hasan ibn al-Haytham, born in Basra, in what is now Iraq, in about 965. He spent much of his working life in Cairo, then the capital of the Fatimid state. According to a story told by later writers, he first came to Egypt with a bold promise: he claimed that the Nile's flood could be controlled by works built in the south. When he travelled up the river and saw the size of the task, the story goes, he realised that the plan was impossible, and to escape the anger of the caliph he pretended to be mad until the ruler's death. Whether every detail of this story is true is uncertain. What is certain is that in Cairo he produced a body of work that would shape the study of light for centuries.
[3] His greatest achievement, the Book of Optics, began by rejecting the idea of rays leaving the eye. Light, he argued, travels from luminous sources such as the sun or a flame, strikes objects, and is reflected from every point on them in straight lines; vision occurs when some of this light enters the eye. He supported his argument not only with reasoning but with observation. Anyone who looks at the sun, he noted, feels pain in the eye, which suggests that something is entering the eye from outside rather than leaving it.
[4] What makes Ibn al-Haytham remarkable is less any single conclusion than the way he reached his conclusions. Again and again, he designed arrangements of equipment to test his claims. He passed light through narrow openings, observed it in darkened rooms and set up tubes and screens to show that light moves in straight lines. In one well-known set of observations, he noted that when light from several lamps passed through a small hole into a dark room, each lamp produced its own separate patch of light on the far wall, and that covering one lamp removed only its patch. The lights, in other words, did not mix in the air. Such experiments could be repeated by anyone with the patience to build the equipment, and that was precisely the point: a claim about nature, in his view, had to be checked against nature.
[5] He was equally clear about the limits of authority. In one of his works, he wrote that a person who studies the writings of scholars should not simply trust them, but should examine them critically and test them, suspecting even his own judgement. To modern ears this may sound obvious. In an age when respect for great ancient authorities ran deep, it was a demanding standard.
[6] The Book of Optics was later translated into Latin, and through that translation it reached scholars in Europe, where it was studied for centuries. Historians still debate how far Ibn al-Haytham's methods resemble the modern scientific method, and it would be a mistake to treat any single person as its inventor. But it is difficult to read his work without recognising a familiar attitude: the conviction that, when an argument and an experiment disagree, it is the argument that must give way.
questions.q: Which choice best describes the author's view of Ibn al-Haytham in the final paragraph?
c: His work shows an attitude toward evidence that modern readers recognise, even if he cannot be called the sole inventor of the scientific method.
His conclusions about light have all been proved wrong.
He was the only scholar of his time who used reasoning.
His ideas were forgotten because they were never translated.
questions.e: The final paragraph balances caution ("a mistake to treat any single person as its inventor") with praise ("a familiar attitude"). His book was translated and studied, so the second choice is false.
ce: Correct: this matches both the praise and the limit in paragraph [6].
The passage presents his ideas positively.
The author does not make this claim.
The Book of Optics was translated into Latin.

items: Read the explanation for every question, including the ones you got right; a lucky guess is not a skill yet.
